subject: Number of latent factors in Exploratory Factor Analysis

messages.author: dae01c57a3c54a3a
messages.subject: Number of latent factors in Exploratory Factor Analysis
parts:
Hi Stan folk,

Just thought I'd check my intuition against the crowd on this one. I have multivariate data and I'm doing exploratory factor analysis where I don't have strong theory guiding the number of latent factors, nor on which items said factors are expected to load. As I understand it, there are two ways to approach this:

1) for each choice of N (number of latent factors, up to a reasonable value for N, like 10, and N being less than the dimensionality of the outcome multivariate), code a model implementing that number of factors, sample against the data, and compare the resulting posterior samples using LOO to choose which choice of N fits best.

2) combine all the above models in a single mixture model that would then yield posterior samples for the mixing proportion of each choice of N.

I tend to prefer (2) as I'm more a fan of parameter estimation over model comparison these days, but anyone have any other thoughts? 

Mike

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Number of latent factors in Exploratory Factor Analysis
parts:
You can also do an approximate Dirichlet process, coding a
larger N with an appropriately near-zero Dirichlet prior.

If you only have N choices, then the mixture might run. It's
one of those nifty mixture of mixtures models. Making a mixture
model's another way to do model comparison. You may find the overall
mixture model itself may work better than any of its components.

- Bob
